v.why: With a skip residual to the output, a pooling edge from node 2 is mostly harmless and the usual drop shrinks.
With a skip carrying the signal directly, a pooling edge costs little and adds smoothing, so the edit is less harmful.
When a strong conv path exists, the direct edge can be a cheap pool with little loss, so the usual penalty is reduced.
A strong direct conv to the output compensates for a weak branch via node 2, so the pool is less costly than usual.
With a strong 3x3 on 1->3, a cheap 1x1 on 2->3 matches a 3x3 closely, so the cheap option suffices (substitution).
A light conv feeding node 1 pairs well with an identity hop to node 2, whereas heavy convs make the skip redundant.
If node 1 is built from a pooled (weak, blurred) input, a strong 3x3 on 1->3 has little rich signal to exploit.
A conv-heavy output makes a 1x1 direct edge redundant, and it replaces a useful skip-like shortcut.
Chaining identity ops along 0->1->2 removes capacity from the deep path, so the skip hurts more.
When the 1->3 conv is strong, a cheap pool on 0->1 loses little, so the edit costs less than usual (substitution).
